title: Walking into the Jazz Party session and Duke's "virgin takes"
summary: Duke pulled Jones to the piano with the red light on; Jones also tells of freezing on the A Train intro on Ellington Is Forever.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Uh-huh.

And there were a whole lot of people there, and there was like a -- it was a party, people were having drinks, because if you remember, Ellington had a lot of tympany and things, you know, he had something else in mind.
Uh-huh.

You know, in the beginning he just happened to look around the room and there his doctor and we -- we were having drinks together, and Duke just pointed to me and told me to come over and sit down. Now, I didn't know that the red light was on, and Irving Townsend was the producer in the booth at that point, you know, and he started -- Duke counted off and started -- oh, what's the -- "Hello, Little Girl," I guess. Jimmy Rushing sang it.
Uh-huh.
And Dizzy Gillespie was playing on it, you know. That was just one take.
That is a fantastic take, too. Were Dizzy and Jimmy Rushing supposed to be on the session, or --
No.
-- was that something that happened the same way as you?
No, none of us was supposed to be on there, you know? The band was there, but -- and the tympany players and all that, but we weren't -- you know, we weren't
supposed to be there. And I doubt if I could do that again.
(Laughter)
Well, that's the kind of performances Duke liked to get, you know.
Yeah. He called them --
Unexpected.
-- virgin takes.
Yeah.

See, if you think about it you get too intellectual, and he's got a point there, too. You know, if you go back and try to outdo yourself, it's just like I was telling Kenny Burrell (PHONETIC) the other night, when we were speaking about the piano solo, I took on the tune, "Orson".
Yes.
And he says, "You want to do it again?" I said no. I've picked up some of Duke's habits.
Uh-huh.
Because then I'll start getting some mental blocks. It's like when I got a mental block and couldn't play the introduction to, "A Train," on the first album.
Uh-huh. That was on the first, "Ellington Is Forever," album.
Yeah. And I just happened to point up to the ceiling and said, "I'm sorry, Edward. I can't get it
Well, maybe Edward didn't want the introduction on that particular rendition.
I couldn't get it together to save me. I'd been playing it all my life, but I had a mental block on it, you know.
